paper_title: Where to Connect? Boosting MLLMs via Dynamic Gated Pathways across ALL ViT and LLM Layers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired into the layer-wise semantics of a large language model. Mainstream MLLMs inject a fixed single-layer visual representation into the LLM and treat all LLM layers as a single consumer, ignoring that different layers demand different visual granularities. Recent multi-layer fusion methods either compress hierarchical features on the encoder side or rely on predefined sparse or hierarchical layer-to-layer connections, and therefore stop short of modeling adaptive cross-layer interactions between the ViT and LLM hierarchies. We address this gap with DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), a routing mechanism that establishes all-to-all connections between every ViT layer and every LLM layer, with each LLM layer dynamically gating its preference over visual layers conditioned on its own semantic state. Built on top of LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B, DGP delivers consistent gains over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline (e.g., +4.2 on SQA$^{I}$, +3.3 on MM-Vet, +3.1 on VizWiz and LLaVA$^{W}$) and surpasses prior multi-layer visual fusion methods on most benchmarks. Layer-wise routing analyses further show that different LLM layers do select different visual granularities on demand, supporting both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed dynamic gated pathways. The code is available: https://github.com/YingyingYan1/DGP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) [3, 16, 19, 21] encode an image with pretrained vision backbone [31, 32, 42], project the resulting features through an adapter, and inject the visual tokens into language model. In this paradigm, the effectiveness of visual information depends not only on the representational power of the encoder [7, 34, 38], butmore criticallyon where to connect: how the visual tokens are wired into the internal layers of the LLM. As illustrated in Figure 1, attention patterns across ViT layers differ markedly: shallow layers attend to edges, textures, and local details, whereas deeper layers progressively concentrate on small number of semantic anchors. Yet, most MLLMs [2, 10, 26] simply forward the output of one fixed ViT layer (typically the last or penultimate layer) to the LLM, as illustrated in Figure 2(A), effectively *Equal Contribution. Shallow layers show dispersed attention over edges and textures; deeper layers progressively concentrate on few semantic anchors. Figure 2: Strategies for visual token insertion. (A) Fixed single-layer connection. (B) Encoderside fusion of multiple ViT layers into one representation. (C) Predefined sparse or hierarchical connections between ViT and LLM layers. (D) DGP (Ours): dynamic gated pathways between all ViT and all LLM layers. wm denotes the routing weights that LLM layer assigns across all ViT layers. collapsing the image into single-granularity semantic representation. Connecting the LLM only to the terminal deep layer therefore discards shallowand mid-level cues and prevents the LLMs layer-wise semantics from interacting with the full visual hierarchy. Two lines of work have started to expose multi-layer visual features to the LLM, but each falls short on the where to connect question. Encoder-side fusion [4, 20, 23, 36, 39] merges multi-layer features into one representation before the LLM (Figure 2(B)); any dynamism is consumed inside the encoder and cannot adapt to the differentiated demands of individual LLM layers. Predefined sparse or hierarchical connections [8, 30, 37, 43] wire selected ViT layers to specific LLM layers (Figure 2(C)), typically using hand-crafted connection patterns or fixed hierarchical mappings. CLI [5] introduces adaptive gating conditioned on the current LLM state, but operates over sampled ViT layers and designated LLM injection points. Neither category explicitly models the adaptive, dynamic cross-layer interactions between all ViT layers and all LLM layers that the question of where to connect demands. Predictive coding in visual neuroscience suggests that perception is not unidirectional feed-forward process but hierarchical feedback loop that continuously modulates activations across layers [33]. We take this as inspiration to revisit visual token injection: visual evidence should not be delivered in one shot through fixed pathway, but should keep participating in the LLMs representation updates through dynamic cross-layer pathways. Building on this view, we introduce DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), which connects all ViT layers to all LLM layers via learned, dynamically gated routes (Figure 2(D)). Concretely, the outputs of different ViT layers act as candidate representations at varying granularities. At every LLM layer, DGP produces routing distribution over all ViT layers from the current hidden state, aggregates the candidates via gated weighted fusion, and injects the result back into the layers visual hidden states through residual connection. The hierarchical visual evidence keeps supplying cues for language reasoning, while the LLMs layer-wise semantic state drives the preference over visual hierarchies, yielding cross-layer, progressively evolving visionlanguage interaction that integrates low-level details and high-level semantics on demand at different decoding depths. We instantiate DGP on top of LLaVA-1.5 [26] and further validate it on Qwen3-VL-2B [3] and LLaVANeXT [27]. Across wide range of multimodal benchmarks, DGP yields consistent improvements over baselines and outperforms prior multi-layer visual feature utilization methods. The learned routing patterns confirm that different LLM layers indeed prefer different visual granularities, alleviating the information bottleneck of fixed single-layer fusion. Our contributions are: 2 We reframe visual information injection in MLLMs around the question of where to connect, and show that fixed single-layer inputs and predefined sparse or hierarchical connections cannot match the differentiated demands of hierarchical ViT representations and layer-wise LLM semantics. We propose DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), an all-to-all cross-layer connection mechanism in which every LLM layer dynamically gates its preference over every ViT layer conditioned on its current semantic state. We demonstrate the effectiveness and interpretability of DGP on multiple multimodal benchmarks, where layer-wise routing analyses reveal the adaptive, layer-dependent selection behavior of the proposed dynamic gated pathways.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Multimodal Large Language Model typical Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) couples vision encoder, visionlanguage adapter, and large language model: the encoder turns the image into visual tokens, the adapter projects them into the language space, and the LLM consumes the joint visualtextual sequence to generate responses. Existing MLLMs mainly fall into two architectural families: projectorbased decoder-only designs (e.g., LLaVA [26], MiniGPT-4 [44], Qwen-VL [2], InternVL [10]) and cross-attention-based designs (e.g., Flamingo [1]). Current MLLMs use pretrained vision backbones such as CLIP-ViT [32] and SigLIP [42], all of which expose representations of varying granularities across their layers. Yet most pipelines project only single fixed layer into the LLM, so the language model sees only one level of visual abstraction. The visual connection mechanism is not merely cross-modal interface: it determines whether the rich, hierarchical visual representations can be accessed and reused inside the LLM. 2.2 Connection Strategies for Visual Token Insertion Different ViT layers carry different semantic granularities: shallow layers retain local textures and spatial details, while middle and deep layers progressively encode object structures and high-level semantics [6]. single deep layer is not always the best choice [6], and exploiting the visual hierarchy depends as much on how layers are connected to the LLM as on which layers are selected [24]. The crux, in other words, is to establish effective connections between vision-encoder layers and LLM layersi.e., the where to connect problem. Prior efforts can be grouped into two categories. Unified Encoder-side Connections. Methods in this category fuse multi-layer visual features on the encoder side and pass single unified representation to the LLM. DenseConnector [39] concatenates features from different ViT layers along the token or channel dimension. MMFuser [4] uses deep-layer features as queries to pull fine-grained information from shallow layers. IGVA [20] and TGIF [23] adjust ViT-layer weights conditioned on the instruction. CCRA [36] combines several attention mechanisms for text-conditioned regionsemantic alignment. While these designs improve multi-layer feature utilization, the entire fusion happens before the LLM; the LLM still receives one homogenized input and cannot reach back into the visual hierarchy as decoding progresses. Predefined Sparse or Hierarchical Connections. Methods in this category route hierarchical visual information to different LLM layers. DeepStack [30] distributes visual tokens across decoder depths according to fixed hierarchical schedule. Sparse Shortcuts [43] wires ViT and LLM layers through predefined connection patterns. EVLM [8] feeds multi-layer ViT features into different gated cross-attention layers. CLI [5] applies adaptive gating at sampled vision layers and designated LLM injection points, rather than treating every ViTLLM pair as candidate connection. more recent line of work [37] selects and fuses hierarchical visual features conditioned on each LLM layers representation. Although these methods begin to acknowledge the hierarchical correspondence between vision and language, most still rely on hand-crafted connection patterns or fixed layer-tolayer mappings, and few of them simultaneously realize (i) all-to-all cross-layer connectivity, (ii) routing weights driven by the current LLM-layer state, and (iii) end-to-end training with stable routing distributionthe design point that DGP targets. 3 Figure 3: Overview of DGP. (A) At every LLM layer, the Dynamic Gated Pathways module routes over all ViT layers conditioned on the current language-layer state, aggregates the selected visual features, and injects them back into the LLM hidden states through gated residual connection establishing all-to-all cross-layer connections between ViT and LLM. (B) Inside the module, ViT layer summaries serve as keys/values and the language-layer state as the query; shared cross-attention followed by layer-specific routing MLP produces the per-layer routing weights. Weight Matrix(m) denotes the routing weights of LLM layer over all ViT layers. In summary, existing methods either compress the visual hierarchy into single pre-LLM representation, or wire it into the LLM through predefined sparse or hierarchical connections; neither answers where to connect via dynamic cross-layer interactions between all ViT layers and all LLM layers. We close this gap with DGP, which establishes adaptive, all-to-all connections between ViT and LLM layers through dynamic gated pathways.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Settings Implementation Details and Training Recipe. We follow the LLaVA-1.5 [26] training recipe, using CLIP-ViT-L/14-336 [32] as the vision encoder and Vicuna as the LLM backbone. Training proceeds in two stages: pre-training (PT) on LLaVA-558K [26] and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on LLaVA-mixed-665K [26]. Because DGP interacts with the hidden states at every LLM layer, both stages jointly optimize the LLM together with the newly introduced DGP modules. The vision encoder is kept frozen throughout, and each stage is trained for one epoch. All hyperparameters follow LLaVA-1.5: AdamW with cosine scheduling (warmup ratio 0.03), batch sizes of 256/128 and learning rates of 1 103/2 105 for PT/SFT, respectively. The routing MLP uses hidden dimension of 1024, and the residual gate is initialized to 0.3. Following TGIF [23], the entropy regularizer uses λ = 0.01 during PT and is disabled (λ = 0) during SFT so routing can specialize. More hyperparameter sensitivity results are provided in Appendix C. Benchmarks. We evaluate on two complementary suites of multimodal benchmarks. Academic VQA covers GQA [15], SciQA-IMG [29], VQAv2 [13], and VizWiz [14]. Instruction-following / LMM benchmarks cover SEED-Bench (SEED/SEEDI ) [18], LLaVA-Wild [25], MM-Vet [40], MMBench [28], and POPE [22], jointly probing multimodal comprehension, fine-grained perception, and hallucination resistance. Baselines. We compare DGP against two groups of baselines. The first group consists of generalpurpose MLLMs: BLIP-2 [19], InstructBLIP [11], Shikra [9], IDEFICS [17], Qwen-VL [2], and LLaVA-1.5 [26]. The second group focuses on multi-layer visual feature utilization: MMFuser [4], Dense Connector [39], DeepStack-L [30], Sparse Shortcuts [43], IGVA [20], and TGIF [23]. For fair comparison, we focus on methods that share the Vicuna backbone and the LLaVA-1.5 configuration. Table 1 compares DGP with mainstream MLLMs and multi-layer visual feature utilization methods under Vicuna-7B and 13B settings. Taking Vicuna-7B as an illustrative example, DGP consistently improves over the LLaVA-1.5 baselinemost prominently on VizWiz (+3.1), SQAI (+4.2), LLaVAW (+3.1), and MM-Vet (+3.3)with similar trends on the remaining benchmarks. Against the strongest multi-layer baselines, DGP attains the best score on GQA, SQAI , SEED, LLaVAW , MM-Vet, and MMBCN , suggesting that compressing the visual hierarchy on the encoder side or using predefined sparse or hierarchical connections is insufficient to capture the full interaction between hierarchical visual evidence and the layer-wise LLM state. Table 4 ablates the two key ingredients of DGPgated routing and entropy regularizationand keeps uniform average over the 24 ViT layers as control, so as to disentangle gains coming from using more visual layers from those coming from where to connect. Adding gated routing alone already yields consistent improvements over the LLaVA-1.5 baseline on most benchmarks. By contrast, uniform average fusion without gated routing hurts performance on most benchmarks relative to the baseline. Equal-weight mixing across the visual hierarchy appears to blend incompatible granularities and weaken fine-grained evidence, whereas gated routing keeps connectivity selective and conditioned on the language-layer state. Stacking the entropy regularizer on top of gated routing brings further gain, indicating that well-spread routing distribution prevents collapse onto few visual layers and stabilizes training. Layer-wise Gated Pathway Analysis. To inspect what DGP actually learns, we visualize the routing weights of every LLM layer over the ViT layers. Figure 5(A) shows clearly non-uniform, layerdependent distribution: DGP neither fixates on the last ViT layer nor degenerates into uniform average. Middle ViT layers are activated most frequently, suggesting that they offer useful trade-off between local structure and high-level semantics. Shallow and deep features are also selected by certain LLM layers, confirming that the model dynamically reaches into different visual granularities according to where it is in decoding rather than relying on single visual layer. Figure 5(B) zooms in on representative LLM layers. Their routing curves peak at different positions: LLM layer 1 favors shallow-to-middle ViT layers, LLM layer 20 leans toward shallow features, whereas LLM layers 22 and 32 peak at mid-deep and deep ViT layers, respectively. The curves are typically multimodal rather than unimodal or flat, showing that DGP selectively combines several visual layers per LLM layer and that different LLM layers prefer different visual granularities depending on their language state. These visualizations confirm that DGP discovers non-uniform, dynamic ViTLLM connection patterns, exploiting the complementarity of the visual hierarchy. Task-aware Gated Pathway Analysis. We next ask whether the routing also adapts to the task itself. Figure 5(C) plots the routing weights of LLM layer 21 across benchmarks: each benchmark induces distinct visual-layer profile. LLaVAW and VizWiz allocate more mass to mid-level features, in line with the need to balance object-level semantics and local visual cues for open-ended QA and real-world understanding, whereas SQAI additionally puts noticeable weight on shallow ViT layer 2, reflecting the fine-grained details required in scientific reasoning. Figure 5(D) zooms one level further down: even within single benchmark, individual samples exhibit substantial routing diversity, indicating that DGPs adaptivity goes beyond benchmark-level differences and operates at the sample level. Figure 6 fixes the image and varies the question. For questions about attribute recognition or smallregion details, DGP activates shallow or shallow-to-middle ViT featureslayers that preserve edges, textures and local spatial structure. For questions that rely more on global semantics or abstract reasoningpainting identification, historical significance, action understandingthe routing weight peaks instead at mid-deep or deep ViT layers. For open-ended questions such as describe the image in detail, which require both local details and holistic semantics, the routing distribution naturally widens into broader multimodal shape that simultaneously taps multiple visual hierarchies. These patterns indicate that DGPs routing is dynamically conditioned on the layer-wise linguistic context and semantic state of the LLM, rather than being determined solely by fixed visual-layer priors. DGPs LLM-layerspecific features instead show clearly more stable spatial structure, sharper subject contours, and lower background noise, preserving local details such as spoon edges and building boundaries. Crucially, the fused features differ across LLM layers 1, 18, and 28, confirming that DGP generates differentiated visual representations via dynamic routing rather than collapsing into fixed averaging pattern. Overall, DGP strengthens global semantics while keeping shallow and middle-layer cues intact, mitigating both the information bottleneck of fixed single-layer features and the noise accumulation of naive averaging.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we reframe visual information injection in MLLMs around the question of where to connect, and argue that fixed single-layer inputs or predefined sparse or hierarchical connections cannot match the differentiated demands of hierarchical ViT representations and layer-wise LLM semantics. We answer this question with DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), an all-to-all cross-layer connection mechanism in which each LLM layer adaptively gates its preference over every ViT layer based on its current semantic state, integrating multi-granularity visual information on demand at every decoding depth. DGP delivers consistent gains across broad set of multimodal benchmarks, while routing analyses and feature visualizations show that it learns interpretable, layer-dependent connection patterns that explain where the gains come from.

sections.title: B Training Configuration and Benchmark Descriptions
sections.content: B.1 Training Configuration Table 6 lists the detailed training hyperparameters for the pre-training (PT) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stages. We follow the LLaVA-1.5 training recipe, using CLIP-ViT-L/14-336 as the vision encoder and Vicuna as the LLM backbone. The vision encoder is kept frozen throughout both stages, each trained for one epoch. The entropy regularizer is enabled during PT to stabilize routing distributions, and disabled during SFT to allow task-specific specialization. All training and efficiency measurements are conducted on NVIDIA L40-48GB GPUs. Backbone Selection Rationale. Our primary experiments are conducted under the LLaVA-1.5 framework, which remains widely adopted open-source baseline in the research community. Specifically, we select Vicuna-v1.5 (7B/13B) as the LLM backbone and adopt the standard LLaVA-1.5 training data (LLaVA-558K for PT and LLaVA-mixed-665K for SFT). This design choice serves two purposes: (i) reproducibility, as all components are publicly available and well-documented; and (ii) fair comparison with modern multi-layer visual fusion methods (e.g., MMFuser [4], IGVA [20], TGIF [23]) that likewise build upon LLaVA-1.5. By holding the backbone architecture, training data, and recipe constant, any observed performance improvement can be cleanly attributed to the proposed DGP module itself, rather than to differences in the underlying LLM, vision encoder, or training corpus. B.2 Benchmark Descriptions To validate the effectiveness of DGP under varying visual granularity requirements, we adopt two complementary suites of multimodal benchmarks. Different tasks exhibit significantly different demands on visual granularity: fine-grained OCR and attribute recognition rely more on shallow local features, while scene understanding and abstract reasoning require deep global semantics. This diversity in granularity requirements directly motivates the design of DGPs dynamic gated pathwaysenabling different LLM layers to adaptively select the visual granularity that best matches their current needs. sections.title: C Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis
sections.content: This section analyzes the design choices of key hyperparameters in DGP, including the entropy regularization coefficient λ, the routing MLP hidden dimension h, and the gating initialization value γinit. 16 Entropy Regularization Coefficient λ. The entropy regularizer discourages routing collapse onto small subset of visual layers. We adopt the same stage-wise schedule as TGIF [23]: λ = 0.01 during pre-training to encourage exploration across layers, and no entropy regularization during supervised fine-tuning (equivalently λ = 0) so routing can specialize to downstream tasks. Routing MLP Hidden Dimension h. The routing MLP maps the 4096-dimensional routing feature to 24-dimensional layer weight distribution. To balance expressiveness and computational efficiency, we set the intermediate hidden dimension to = 1024, aligning with the ViT hidden dimension. This design ensures that the routing network has sufficient nonlinear modeling capacity while avoiding the additional computational overhead of using the full LLM dimension (4096). Gating Initialization γinit. The gating coefficient γl = σ(al) controls the injection strength of visual information at the l-th layer, where al is learnable scalar. We use default gate initialization of γinit = 0.3 and set the gate learning rate to 5 103. An initialization value that is too small leads to insufficient visual injection, causing the model to degenerate toward pure language model behavior; an initialization value that is too large may introduce excessive noise in early training, affecting convergence stability. sections.title: E Additional Analysis
sections.content: E.1 Effect of Unfreezing Vision Encoder natural question is whether unfreezing the vision encoder during training could further improve performance. Table 10 compares DGP with frozen versus unfrozen ViT. Interestingly, unfreezing the 17 ViT leads to performance drops on most benchmarks (e.g., GQA, VQAv2, VizWiz, SEEDI , POPE), while only MMB shows improvement. We attribute this to key property of our method: the dynamic routing mechanism relies on the stable semantic hierarchy across ViT layersshallow layers encode textures and edges, while deeper layers capture high-level semantics. This layerwise division of labor is established during CLIPs large-scale pre-training on 400M image-text pairs. When the ViT is fine-tuned on our comparatively smaller dataset, this hierarchical structure may drift, causing the router to chase moving target. In contrast, freezing the ViT provides stable visual foundation, allowing the router and fusion modules to learn consistent layer-selection strategies. sections.title: F Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: The Dynamic Gated Pathways module is designed to be plug-and-play: it introduces only lightweight, layer-wise routing components that interface with the LLM hidden states, without modifying the vision encoder or the LLM architecture itself. This modularity suggests that DGP should generalize across vision encoders and LLM backbones, adaptively selecting appropriate visual granularities regardless of the specific encoderdecoder pairing. In this work, we validate DGP primarily under the LLaVA-1.5 setting (CLIP + Vicuna-7B/13B) and further on smaller-scale alternative frameworks, including Qwen3-VL-2B (SigLIP2 + Qwen3-1.7B) and LLaVA-NeXT (AnyRes tiling). Due to resource and time constraints, however, experiments on 19 larger LLMs (30B+), broader families of vision encoders, and larger-scale multimodal corpora remain limited. Extending validation along these axes constitutes our primary future work. We anticipate that the dynamic routing mechanism will remain effectiveand potentially more beneficialas model capacity and data scale increase, since richer language representations should enable even finer-grained visual-layer selection.

sections.title: G Broader Impacts
sections.content: This work improves hierarchical visual access in MLLMs, which may benefit applications such as accessibility tools and educational assistants. At the same time, stronger visual reasoning could be misused for surveillance or misleading content, and DGP may inherit biases from the pretrained vision and language backbones it fine-tunes. We therefore view DGP as an architectural improvement for research use under the licenses and safety practices of the host models.

sections.title: H Use of Large Language Models
sections.content: For transparency, we disclose that general-purpose large language models (LLMs) were used during the preparation of this manuscript solely as writing-assistance tools to improve the clarity, concision, and grammaticality of the text. Their use was restricted to language-level editing: rewriting sentences for readability, tightening phrasing, polishing transitions, and correcting typos. No LLM was used to generate scientific claims, design experiments, produce technical content, or decide on methodology; all results, figures, analyses, and conclusions were conceived and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content of every paragraph.
